person.name: Grace_Hopper
person.summary: Grace Hopper was an American computer scientist, mathematician, and United States Navy rear admiral. She programmed the Harvard Mark I, developed compiler systems, led work on FLOW-MATIC, and helped create COBOL.

events.title: Born into a New York Family
events.description: She was the eldest of three children in a family of Scottish and Dutch descent.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, USA

events.title: Graduates Phi Beta Kappa from Vassar
events.description: Hopper graduates Phi Beta Kappa from Vassar College with a bachelor's degree in mathematics and physics.

images.caption: Vassar College Main Building and campus drive
images.creator: BappleBusiness

events.title: Marries New York Professor Vincent Hopper
events.description: In 1930, she married a New York University professor.

events.title: Earns a Doctorate at Yale
events.description: Hopper received her Ph.D. in mathematics from Yale University under the direction of Øystein Ore. Her dissertation was titled New Types of Irreducibility Criteria.
events.background:
Yale’s graduate mathematics program followed Hopper’s undergraduate work at Vassar College, where she had studied mathematics and physics. She completed a master’s degree at Yale in 1930. That same year, she married Vincent Foster Hopper, a New York University professor. The marriage ended in divorce in 1945. She kept the Hopper surname for the rest of her life.

Her doctoral work overlapped with the beginning of her academic career at Vassar. She joined the faculty there in 1931 as a mathematics teacher. The college promoted her to associate professor in 1941. Her Yale training covered mathematics and mathematical physics. Her dissertation was published in the same year that she completed the degree.

The years at Vassar gave Hopper a long base in teaching before wartime service redirected her work toward machines. She later declined a full professorship at Vassar to remain at Harvard as a research fellow working under a Navy contract. The Harvard Computation Laboratory employed her after the war through 1949. Her later explanations of computer programming often returned to a teacher’s concern that data-processing workers should be able to write instructions in English words.

In 2024, the IEEE dedicated a marker at the University of Pennsylvania for Hopper’s later work on the A-0 compiler. The marker cited her influence on young engineers. Yale later renamed one of its residential colleges Grace Hopper College in her honor.

background_images.caption: Grace Hopper College, Yale University. Elm Street facade, New Haven, Connecticut
background_images.creator: Kenneth C. Zirkel

events.title: Joins the Navy Reserve Through WAVES
events.description: Hopper takes leave from Vassar College and joins the United States Navy Reserve through WAVES in 1943. The Navy had earlier rejected her because of her age, weight-to-height ratio, and Vassar work. It grants her an exemption from the minimum weight requirement.

images.caption: 1943 U.S. Navy WAVES recruitment poster
images.creator: John Philip Falter, US Naval Reserve (USNR)

events.title: Begins Programming the Harvard Mark I
events.description: Hopper graduates first in her class at the Naval Reserve Midshipmen's School in Northampton, Massachusetts. The Navy assigns her to the Bureau of Ships Computation Project at Harvard University in Cambridge. She joins the Mark I programming staff led by Howard H. Aiken.

images.caption: Harvard Mark I automatic sequence controlled calculator
images.creator: Capvideo

events.background:
Harvard’s wartime computation work grew from a problem Aiken had faced while studying vacuum-tube conduction for his Harvard physics doctorate. He needed numerical solutions to differential equations. He looked to Charles Babbage’s difference engine for a way to shift repetitive calculations from people to a machine. The resulting project was first called the Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator, or ASCC. It later became known as the Harvard Mark I.

IBM supplied the engineering, construction, and funding for the machine. The completed computer was installed at Harvard in February 1944. Its arrival placed a large-scale programmable machine inside a university computation project tied to the Navy’s Bureau of Ships. Richard Milton Bloch and Robert Campbell also came to the project as programmers. The work demanded methods for giving the machine a sequence of operations and checking the results of long calculations.

Aiken’s laboratory continued to build a series of successors after the first machine entered service. He completed the Harvard Mark II in 1947. The Mark III later used some electronic components and magnetic-drum memory. The Mark IV was all-electronic and also used magnetic-core memory. The work at the Computation Laboratory produced three papers co-authored by Hopper and Aiken. In 1947, Aiken also established a Harvard master’s program in computer science, nearly a decade before such programs became common at other universities. Many later computer scientists completed doctoral dissertations under his direction.

events.title: Writes the Harvard Mark I Manual
events.description: At Harvard University, Hopper prepares A Manual of Operation for the Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator. The manual explains the operation of the Mark I computer.

images.caption: Harvard Mark I computer on display
images.creator: Waldir Pimenta

events.title: Joins the UNIVAC I Development Team
events.description: Hopper joined the Eckert–Mauchly Computer Corporation as a senior mathematician and began work on the UNIVAC I.

images.caption: Grace Hopper at the UNIVAC keyboard, 1957
images.creator: Unknown authorUnknown author

events.title: Completes the A-0 Compiler System
events.description: Hopper finishes a program linker for the A-0 System in 1952. She calls the program linker a compiler.

event_class.title: A-0 System
event_class.description: A-0 is a link-loader that translates mathematical notation into machine code and combines program routines for the UNIVAC.

events.title: Leads Automatic Programming at Eckert–Mauchly
events.description: Eckert–Mauchly chooses Hopper to lead its automatic-programming department in 1954. She leads the release of compiled languages including FLOW-MATIC.

event_class.title: FLOW-MATIC
event_class.description: FLOW-MATIC is a compiler-based language that lets business users write data-processing instructions with English-like words.
event_class.impact: Its language design supplies a major foundation for the later COBOL specification.

events.title: Helps Develop the COBOL Language
events.description: In spring 1959, Hopper serves as a technical consultant to [[CODASYL]]. The committee develops COBOL as a machine-independent programming language. Jean E. Sammet is among its developers.

images.caption: COBOL display at the Museum of American History
images.creator: blakespot

event_class.title: COBOL
event_class.description: COBOL is a machine-independent business programming language that uses English-like words for data processing instructions.
event_class.impact: COBOL becomes widely used for business data processing across government and industry.

CODASYL.explanation: The Conference on Data Systems Languages was an industry consortium formed to develop common data-processing languages.

events.background:
Commercial computer makers had produced separate programming systems for their own machines. Hopper’s earlier FLOW-MATIC supplied an English-worded model for data-processing work. IBM’s COMTRAN supplied another set of ideas. The language effort drew on both systems. Its planned users handled payroll, taxes, records, and other large bodies of business data. Hopper had argued that many data-processing workers could write English statements more easily than symbolic instructions. Her A-0 work had already translated mathematical notation into machine code.

Jean E. Sammet arrived with experience from Sperry Gyroscope, where she had supervised the first scientific programming group. In 1955, she had entered 20 binary instructions by hand over three days to create the basic loader for the SPEEDAC computer. At Sylvania Electric Products in Needham, Massachusetts, she oversaw software development for the MOBIDIC project under Carl Hammer. During 1959, Sammet and five other programmers prepared much of the language’s design in a proposal completed over two weeks. Sylvania’s U.S. government clients accepted the proposal.

The resulting work extended Hopper’s FLOW-MATIC approach and incorporated ideas from IBM’s COMTRAN. Sammet later joined IBM in 1961. She developed FORMAC there in 1962 for symbolic manipulation of mathematical formulas. Hopper’s later Navy Programming Languages Group built validation software for COBOL and its compiler. Its conformance tests helped bring the differing versions used by major computer vendors closer together. The National Bureau of Standards took over the tests and their administration in the 1980s.

background_images.caption: Pronounced "Moby Dick" perhaps? A model of a "portable" computer for the US Army c.1967.
background_images.creator: Erik Pitti from San Diego, CA, USA

events.title: Leads Navy Programming Languages Group
events.description: Hopper directs the Navy Programming Languages Group in the Navy Office of Information Systems Planning. Her group develops COBOL validation software and compiler tests for Navy standardization.

events.title: Is Promoted to Rear Admiral
events.description: Hopper is promoted to rear admiral, lower half, on November 8, 1985. Congress approves her continued active duty beyond the normal retirement age.

events.title: Retires from the United States Navy
events.description: Hopper retires from the Navy after more than 42 years of service. She receives the Defense Distinguished Service Medal aboard USS Constitution in Boston. She is the Navy's oldest serving officer at the time.

events.title: Receives National Medal of Technology
events.description: Hopper receives the National Medal of Technology in 1991. The award recognizes her work on programming languages that simplified computer technology and made it more accessible.

events.title: Dies at Home in Arlington
events.description: Hopper died in her sleep at her home in Arlington County, Virginia, on New Year’s Day 1992.

images.caption: Gravesite of U.S. Navy Admiral Grace Hopper
images.creator: Arlington National Cemetery

events.background:
Digital Equipment Corporation hired Hopper after she left the Navy. Rita Yavinsky initially offered her a position. Hopper insisted on completing the usual formal interview. She joked that she would work alternating Thursdays. She proposed being displayed as a computing pioneer in the company museum. She also asked for a generous salary and an unlimited expense account. DEC hired her full time as a Principal Corporate Consulting Engineer. The role carried the standing of a tech-track senior vice president.

At DEC, Hopper represented the company at industry forums and served on industry committees. She visited most of the company’s engineering facilities. Audiences generally gave her standing ovations after her remarks. Her talks drew on the early history of computing and on ways vendors could make systems easier for users. She urged young people to attempt difficult work. She said she would support them and later “stir ’em up” so they would continue taking chances.

Hopper wore her Navy full dress uniform for these appearances. Department of Defense policy did not permit the uniform for a former officer in that setting. Her demonstrations included pieces of wire measuring just under one foot. She called each piece a nanosecond because light travels that far in a nanosecond in a vacuum. She explained that signals move more slowly through actual wire. She later used the wires to explain why computers needed to be small for speed. At DEC talks, she also handed out packets of pepper as picoseconds. She remained in her DEC post until the end of her life.
